en.title: Marine Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What marine engineering covers, how the degree and sea-going certificates are organised, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What marine engineering is
sections.text:
Marine engineering is the branch of engineering concerned with the machinery, systems and structure of ships and other marine craft, and with offshore installations. A marine engineer designs, operates, maintains and repairs main engines, boilers, pumps, piping, electrical plant, steering gear, refrigeration and control systems. It overlaps naval architecture, which deals mainly with hull form, stability and the behaviour of the ship as a whole.

There are two career routes. One is going to sea as an engineering officer, keeping the plant running and safe. The other is working ashore in design offices, shipyards, classification societies, engine makers or offshore companies. Both rest on the same principles, which is why the course begins with mathematics, mechanics and fluids.

These summaries teach principles. They do not replace classification society rules, flag state regulations or the judgement of a qualified engineer. Rules differ by country and change over time, so check the current edition of whatever document applies to you.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length, award and title differ by country and by institution, so check your own handbook rather than assuming.

In Nigeria a BEng usually takes five years and includes industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnics usually award an ND, then an HND after supervised industrial work. The engineering profession is regulated by COREN, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria. In the United Kingdom a BEng usually takes three years and an MEng four, with Scotland often a year longer; professional registration runs through the Engineering Council and institutions such as the IMechE or IMarEST. Ghana, Kenya and other countries have their own patterns.

Separately, an officer who keeps watch in a ship’s engine room needs a certificate of competency issued by a maritime administration under the STCW Convention of the International Maritime Organization. A degree alone does not give that certificate. It needs approved training, sea time and examinations, and the ship’s flag state endorses it for service on board.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage builds the tools: engineering mathematics, statics and dynamics, fluid mechanics, thermodynamics and heat transfer, materials science, electrical and electronic principles, and drawing with computer-aided design. Two subjects then give the vocabulary of the ship itself: introduction to marine engineering, and ship construction and stability fundamentals, covering hull structure, compartments, stability and load lines.

The core stage turns to machinery. Marine diesel engines come first, because they drive most ships today. Then boilers and steam systems, steam and gas turbines, propulsion with propellers and shafting, pumps, piping and valves, and auxiliary machinery. Electrical power systems, automation and control, and refrigeration and air conditioning follow, because modern ships are controlled and monitored as integrated plants. Fuels, lubricants and combustion, corrosion and material protection, and maintenance and condition monitoring explain how machinery is kept efficient and reliable.

The final core subjects look outward: ship safety, fire protection and life-saving; maritime environmental protection; maritime law, classification and certification; professional practice, ethics and regulation; and research methods leading to a final-year project.

At master’s level come advanced marine thermodynamics and energy systems, computational fluid dynamics, alternative fuels and decarbonisation, and research methods for a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Draw the system before you calculate. A rough sketch of a cooling water circuit or a fuel line makes the numbers mean something, and reading piping and instrumentation diagrams is a skill employers expect.

Carry units through every line: pressure in bar or pascal, power in kilowatt, specific fuel consumption in grams per kilowatt hour. Then ask whether the answer is the right size. Learn typical values, such as the efficiency of a large slow-speed diesel engine or the pressure of a boiler, so that a wrong result stands out.

Treat the ship as a laboratory. Engine room visits, simulator sessions and sea time teach more than diagrams alone. Keep a notebook of machinery, readings and faults. Work through past questions and explain your answers aloud, because at sea you will have to explain a fault to a chief engineer.

en.title: Engineering mathematics for marine engineers
en.short: Algebra, trigonometry, calculus, differential equations and numerical methods for ship machinery.

sections.heading: Algebra and trigonometry
sections.text:
Algebra rearranges formulas and solves for an unknown. In machinery work, units must match before substituting. If an engine develops P = 1,200 kW at specific fuel consumption sfc = 190 g/kWh, fuel mass flow is m = P × sfc = 1,200 × 190 = 228,000 g/h = 228 kg/h, or 228 ÷ 3,600 = 0.0633 kg/s.

Trigonometry relates angles and sides. It is used for resolving forces, propeller blade angles and tank sounding tables. Sine, cosine and tangent come from right triangles; the sine rule and cosine rule handle other triangles. A sounding table converts measured depth to volume.

sections.heading: Calculus and equations
sections.text:
Calculus studies change. The derivative gives a rate, such as how fuel flow changes with load. The integral adds small contributions, such as work = ∫ F dx or volume from a curve. The derivative of position with time is velocity; the second derivative is acceleration.

A differential equation links a quantity to its rate of change. A first-order equation such as dT/dt = −k(T − T∞) describes cooling towards surrounding temperature T∞; its solution is an exponential. Marine engineers use such models for control, vibration and transient machinery behaviour. Initial conditions fix the constants.

sections.heading: Numerical methods
sections.text:
Numerical methods give approximate answers when algebra is difficult. Newton-Raphson finds a root using xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ) ÷ f′(xₙ). For f(x) = x² − 2, start x₀ = 1: x₁ = 1 − (−1) ÷ 2 = 1.5; x₂ = 1.5 − 0.25 ÷ 3 = 1.4167.

The trapezoidal rule approximates an integral by joining points with straight lines; Simpson’s rule uses parabolas and is often more accurate for smooth curves. Euler’s method steps forward through a differential equation. Always check units, convergence and the size of the error. Numerical results are estimates, not exact proofs.

keyPoints: Check units before substituting into any formula; convert kg/h to kg/s by dividing by 3,600.
Trigonometry resolves forces and angles using sine, cosine and tangent, plus the sine and cosine rules.
The derivative is a rate of change; the integral accumulates small contributions such as work = ∫ F dx.
A first-order differential equation such as dT/dt = −k(T − T∞) has an exponential solution.
Newton-Raphson uses xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ) ÷ f′(xₙ); the trapezoidal and Simpson’s rules approximate integrals.
Numerical methods give approximate answers, so check convergence, error and units.

en.title: Engineering mechanics: statics and dynamics
en.short: Forces, moments, equilibrium, friction, motion, work and power applied to ship structures and machinery.

sections.heading: Forces and moments
sections.text:
A force is a push or pull in newtons (N). It has size, direction and point of application, so it is a vector. A moment is the turning effect of a force: M = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance to the line of action. The unit is N·m.

Example: a 12 kN force acts 2.5 m from a bracket. M = 12 × 2.5 = 30 kN·m. Hull girders, engine seatings and crane pedestals resist such moments.

sections.heading: Equilibrium and friction
sections.text:
A body in static equilibrium has zero resultant force and moment: ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0. Free-body diagrams show loads and reactions. Friction opposes sliding. Static friction reaches a limit Fmax = μsN; kinetic friction is Fk = μkN, where μ is the coefficient; N the normal force.

Example: a 500 N crate on a deck with μs = 0.3 starts sliding at Fmax = 0.3 × 500 = 150 N.

sections.heading: Motion and dynamics
sections.text:
Kinematics describes motion. For constant acceleration a: v = u + at and s = ut + ½at²; u, v are initial and final velocity, s displacement, t time. Dynamics links force and motion by Newton’s second law, F = ma, for constant mass. For rotation, torque T = Iα.

Example: a 2,000 kg engine accelerates at 0.5 m/s². Net force = 2,000 × 0.5 = 1,000 N.

sections.heading: Work, energy and power
sections.text:
Work is energy transferred by a force: W = Fd cos θ, in joules (J), where θ is the angle between force and displacement. Kinetic energy is ½mv² and gravitational potential energy is mgh. Power is the rate of doing work: P = W ÷ t = Fv, in watts (W). Propellers absorb shaft power; pumps raise fluid energy.

Example: a 10 kN winch lifts a load 3 m in 6 s. Work = 10,000 × 3 = 30,000 J. Power = 30,000 ÷ 6 = 5,000 W = 5 kW.

keyPoints: For static equilibrium, ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0.
Moment M = F × d, with d perpendicular to the line of action.
Friction limit Fmax = μsN; kinetic friction Fk = μkN.
Constant acceleration: v = u + at and s = ut + ½at².
Newton’s second law F = ma; rotational form T = Iα.
Work W = Fd cos θ; power P = W ÷ t = Fv; kinetic energy ½mv².

en.title: Fluid mechanics fundamentals
en.short: Fluid properties, pressure, buoyancy, continuity, Bernoulli, pipe flow and losses.

sections.heading: Fluid properties and pressure
sections.text:
Fluid mechanics studies liquids and gases at rest and in motion. Density ρ is mass per volume. Relative density compares a liquid with water. Viscosity measures resistance to shear; dynamic viscosity μ has units Pa·s, and kinematic viscosity ν = μ ÷ ρ has units m²/s.

Pressure p is force per area, in pascals. In a static fluid, pressure rises with depth: p = p0 + ρgh, where h is depth below the free surface. Hull plating near the waterline feels greater pressure than higher plating.

sections.heading: Hydrostatics and buoyancy
sections.text:
Hydrostatics treats fluids at rest. A submerged flat surface feels a force equal to pressure at its centroid times area. Buoyancy is the upward force equal to the weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes’ principle).

For a floating ship, displacement equals its weight. Flooding a compartment adds weight and loses buoyancy, changing draught and trim; stability has its own topic.

sections.heading: Flow and energy
sections.text:
Continuity conserves mass flow: ρ1A1V1 = ρ2A2V2. For an incompressible liquid, A1V1 = A2V2, so a smaller pipe area gives higher velocity.

Bernoulli’s equation for steady, frictionless flow along a streamline is p ÷ (ρg) + V² ÷ (2g) + z = constant. It trades pressure, velocity and height. Real flow loses energy to friction, so Bernoulli is an ideal limit.

sections.heading: Pipe flow and losses
sections.text:
Pipe flow is laminar when viscous forces dominate and turbulent when inertia dominates. The Reynolds number Re = ρVD ÷ μ (or VD ÷ ν) indicates the regime; the changeover depends on conditions. Laminar losses vary with velocity; turbulent losses vary with velocity squared. Losses are major (friction in straight pipe) and minor (fittings, bends, valves).

Example: water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) flows at V = 2 m/s in a pipe of diameter D = 0.05 m with μ = 0.001 Pa·s. Re = 1000 × 2 × 0.05 ÷ 0.001 = 100,000, so the flow is turbulent. A pump must supply pressure to overcome friction and minor losses plus lift.

keyPoints: Pressure in a static fluid: p = p0 + ρgh.
Buoyancy equals the weight of fluid displaced; for a floating ship, displacement equals weight.
Continuity: ρ1A1V1 = ρ2A2V2; for incompressible flow A1V1 = A2V2.
Bernoulli for steady frictionless flow: p ÷ (ρg) + V² ÷ (2g) + z = constant.
Reynolds number Re = ρVD ÷ μ = VD ÷ ν indicates laminar or turbulent flow.
Pipe losses are major friction losses and minor losses from fittings; pumps must overcome them.

en.title: Thermodynamics and heat transfer fundamentals
en.short: Energy laws, gas properties, cycles and the three heat transfer modes in marine plant.

sections.heading: Laws and properties
sections.text: Thermodynamics studies energy, heat and work. A system is the matter studied; surroundings are everything else. The first law conserves energy: for a closed system, Q − W = ΔU, where Q is heat added, W is work done by the system and U is internal energy. The second law says entropy of an isolated system cannot fall, so heat cannot flow spontaneously from cold to hot. Properties describe state: pressure p, temperature T, volume V, internal energy U, enthalpy H = U + pV and entropy S. Saturation values for steam are tabulated.

sections.heading: Ideal gases and cycles
sections.text: An ideal gas obeys pV = nRT, where n is amount in moles and R is the molar gas constant. For fixed mass, pV ÷ T is constant. Specific heats cp and cv satisfy cp − cv = R, where R is the specific gas constant for that gas (the molar gas constant divided by the molar mass). A cycle returns the working fluid to its initial state. For a heat engine, thermal efficiency = net work ÷ heat supplied. The Carnot cycle gives the maximum efficiency between reservoirs at absolute temperatures TH and TC: η = 1 − TC ÷ TH. Marine diesel and steam plants fall short of this limit.

sections.heading: Heat transfer modes
sections.text: Conduction is heat flow through matter by molecular vibration. Fourier’s law gives Q ÷ t = kAΔT ÷ L, where k is thermal conductivity, A area and L thickness. Convection moves heat with a fluid; Newton’s law gives Q ÷ t = hAΔT, where h is the convection coefficient. Radiation travels as electromagnetic waves; black-body emission is Q ÷ t = σAT⁴, where σ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant and T is absolute temperature. Example: steel plate k = 45 W/(m·K), A = 0.5 m², L = 0.01 m, ΔT = 20 K. Q ÷ t = 45 × 0.5 × 20 ÷ 0.01 = 45,000 W = 45 kW.

sections.heading: Heat exchangers and plant
sections.text: Heat exchangers transfer heat between two fluids. Rate Q = U A ΔTm, where U is overall coefficient and ΔTm mean temperature difference. Marine examples: jacket-water and oil coolers, boilers, waste-heat recovery. Fouling lowers U.

keyPoints: First law for a closed system: Q − W = ΔU; second law limits heat flow and cycle efficiency.
Ideal gas: pV = nRT, and cp − cv = R, the specific gas constant.
Carnot efficiency between absolute temperatures TH and TC is η = 1 − TC ÷ TH.
Conduction: Q ÷ t = kAΔT ÷ L; convection: Q ÷ t = hAΔT; radiation: Q ÷ t = σAT⁴.
Heat exchanger rate: Q = U A ΔTm, where U is the overall coefficient.
Marine plant uses these ideas in engine cooling, boilers and waste-heat recovery.

en.title: Materials science and engineering materials
en.short: Metals, alloys, polymers and composites: structure, properties, testing, failure and selection.

sections.heading: Structure and properties
sections.text: Properties come from structure. Metals are crystalline: atoms form repeating lattices, and grains are regions with the same orientation. Polymers are long-chain molecules. Composites have a matrix and a reinforcement. Strength is stress at yield or failure; stiffness is resistance to elastic deformation; ductility is strain before fracture; toughness is energy absorbed before fracture; hardness is resistance to indentation. These depend on composition, treatment and temperature.

sections.heading: Metals and alloys
sections.text:
An alloy is a metal with added elements. Mild steel (iron with small carbon) is cheap, strong and weldable, so it is common in ship structures. Stainless steels contain chromium and resist rust. Aluminium alloys are lighter but less stiff. Copper alloys such as bronze and copper-nickel are used in seawater piping and propellers.

Example: volume 0.001 m³. Steel: 7850 × 0.001 = 7.85 kg. Aluminium: 2700 × 0.001 = 2.70 kg. Saving = 5.15 kg, but the aluminium part may need thicker sections.

sections.heading: Polymers and composites
sections.text: Polymers are light and resist water, but they are weaker and less stiff than metals and soften when hot. Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be reshaped; thermosetting polymers set permanently. Composites combine a matrix (the binder) with reinforcement such as glass fibre. Glass-reinforced plastic (GRP) is used for hulls and pipes: the fibres carry load and the matrix holds them.

sections.heading: Testing, failure and selection
sections.text:
A tensile test gives yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and elongation. An impact test measures toughness; hardness tests are quick. Fatigue is failure under repeated stress. Other failures are yielding, ductile or brittle fracture, and creep (slow deformation under sustained load when hot).

Select by load, environment, temperature, cost, weldability and rules. Standards differ by country: ASTM in the United States, EN in Europe, and COREN regulates engineering registration in Nigeria. Classification societies also approve marine components. Check the current code for your vessel and flag state.

keyPoints: Properties depend on structure: metals are crystalline, polymers are long-chain molecules, and composites have a matrix and reinforcement.
Mass = density × volume; 0.001 m³ of steel at 7850 kg/m³ is 7.85 kg, while the same volume of aluminium at 2700 kg/m³ is 2.70 kg.
A tensile test gives yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and elongation, while an impact test gives toughness.
Fatigue is failure under repeated stress and can occur below the yield strength.
Select marine materials by load, environment, temperature, cost, weldability and the applicable code, not by density alone.
Standards and registration differ by country; check the current code and classification society rules.

en.title: Electrical and electronic principles
en.short: DC and AC circuits, magnetism, transformers, machines, semiconductors and shipboard measurement.

sections.heading: DC circuits and magnetism
sections.text: Voltage drives current; current is charge flow; resistance opposes it. Ohm’s law: V = IR. Power: P = VI = I²R. Series resistances add; parallel conductances add, so 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. A current makes a magnetic field. Faraday’s law: changing flux linkage induces an emf (electromotive force); Lenz’s law: the induced effect opposes the change. Example: 12 V across 4 Ω gives I = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 A and P = 12 × 3 = 36 W.

sections.heading: AC circuits and transformers
sections.text: AC alternates sinusoidally. Frequency is cycles per second. For a sine wave, Vrms (root mean square) = Vpeak ÷ √2; rms values give the same heating as DC. Reactance opposes change: XL = 2πfL and XC = 1 ÷ (2πfC). Impedance Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²). A transformer changes voltage by turns ratio: Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns. Ideal power is unchanged, so current changes inversely. Example: 460 primary turns and 230 secondary turns on 230 V give Vs = 230 × 230 ÷ 460 = 115 V.

sections.heading: Motors and generators
sections.text: A motor converts electrical energy to mechanical energy; a generator does the reverse. In a DC machine, a commutator and brushes reverse the coil connections so current or output stays unidirectional. An AC induction motor uses a rotating magnetic field from the stator to induce currents in the rotor; the rotor turns slightly slower than the field, and the difference is slip. Synchronous machines turn at the field speed. Shipboard pumps, winches and steering gear use such machines; isolation and protective earthing are essential.

sections.heading: Semiconductors and measurement
sections.text: A diode conducts one way and rectifies AC to DC. A transistor amplifies or switches; a thyristor switches large currents when triggered. A voltmeter goes in parallel and an ammeter in series. A clamp meter measures current without breaking the circuit. Insulation resistance is measured with the circuit dead. Instruments need calibration. True rms meters suit distorted waveforms. Installation rules differ by country and flag state; in Nigeria, the engineering regulator registers engineers. Check official sources.

keyPoints: V = IR and P = VI = I²R apply to DC circuits.
For a sine wave, Vrms = Vpeak ÷ √2; XL = 2πfL and XC = 1 ÷ (2πfC).
Impedance is Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²).
Ideal transformer voltage ratio: Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns, with power unchanged.
Motors convert electrical energy to mechanical energy; generators do the reverse, and induction motors rely on slip.
Diodes rectify, transistors switch or amplify, and meters must be connected correctly and calibrated.

en.title: Engineering drawing and computer-aided design
en.short: Orthographic views, sections, dimensioning, tolerances, assembly drawings, P&IDs and CAD.

sections.heading: Views and sections
sections.text:
Orthographic projection shows an object as separate front, top and side views, each looking along an axis at right angles to the others. First-angle projection puts each view on the far side of the object; third-angle puts it on the near side. The projection symbol states which system is used.

A section cuts away part of the object to reveal internal detail. The cutting plane is marked, and the cut face is hatched.

sections.heading: Dimensions and tolerances
sections.text:
Dimensioning gives size and position using extension lines, dimension lines, arrows and a numeral. Give each dimension once, on the view that shows the feature clearly. Do not scale a drawing; use the stated dimensions.

A tolerance is the allowed variation from a nominal size. For a shaft of 40.00 mm with limits 39.95 mm and 40.05 mm, the tolerance is 40.05 − 39.95 = 0.10 mm. A clearance fit always leaves a gap; an interference fit always overlaps. Use the standard named on the drawing.

sections.heading: Assembly and P&ID
sections.text:
An assembly drawing shows how parts fit together, with a parts list or bill of materials giving item numbers, descriptions and quantities. It usually omits manufacturing dimensions that belong on detail drawings.

A piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID) is a schematic of a process: pipes, valves, pumps, tanks and instruments. Instrument tags such as FT-101 (flow transmitter) identify each item. P&IDs are not to scale; they show function and connections.

sections.heading: CAD practice
sections.text:
CAD replaces manual drafting with software that stores geometry in a model. A 2D drawing uses layers for lines, dimensions and text. A 3D model can produce orthographic views and sections automatically. Parametric CAD ties dimensions to geometry, so changing a dimension updates the model.

Use the project’s templates and layers, name files clearly and keep revisions. Drawing standards and professional registration differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN regulates engineers, but the drawing standard is usually named in the contract.

keyPoints: Orthographic projection uses separate views at right angles; first-angle places views on the far side, third-angle on the near side.
A section view uses a marked cutting plane and hatching to show internal detail.
Dimension each feature once on the clearest view and never scale the drawing.
Tolerance = upper limit − lower limit; for 40.05 mm and 39.95 mm it is 0.10 mm.
An assembly drawing shows how parts fit and is supported by a bill of materials.
A P&ID is a non-scale schematic showing process connections and instrument tags, while CAD stores geometry in layers and models.

en.title: Introduction to marine engineering
en.short: This summary covers ship types, machinery spaces, main and auxiliary systems, terminology, roles and safety culture.

sections.heading: Ships and spaces
sections.text: Marine engineering is the design, operation and maintenance of the machinery and systems that make a ship work. Common ship types include bulk carriers, which carry dry cargo such as grain or ore; tankers, which carry liquid cargo; container ships, which carry standard boxes; passenger ships; offshore support vessels; and tugs. A machinery space is an enclosed compartment holding propulsion or support equipment. The main one is the engine room; others include the steering gear room and pump room.

sections.heading: Main and auxiliary
sections.text: The main system drives the ship. In most ships today this is a propulsion engine turning a propeller through a shaft, but the principle is simply that the main machinery produces thrust. Auxiliary systems support the main system and the ship: electrical power, steering, fuel supply, lubrication, cooling, ballast, bilge, compressed air and fire systems. A system is a set of connected parts that work together for one duty. Main and auxiliary machinery must be operated as one plant.

sections.heading: Terms and roles
sections.text: Marine terms are precise. Port is the left side facing forward; starboard is the right. Forward is towards the bow, aft towards the stern. Draught is the depth of the hull below the waterline; deadweight is the total mass a ship can carry. The master commands the ship. The chief engineer heads the engine department. Engineer officers of the watch operate and maintain machinery; electro-technical officers handle electrical and control systems; ratings do routine work under supervision.

sections.heading: Safety and profession
sections.text: Safety culture means shared habits. It includes risk assessment, permit to work, short safety briefings, stop-work authority and enclosed-space entry. A permit to work is a written check that hazards are controlled. Case: on a Lagos tug, engineer Chidi briefs the watch before tank entry; gas check, standby person and permit are routine. Marine engineers work for owners, yards, class societies (rule-setting bodies) and regulators. Codes, standards and registration differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN registers engineers. Check current flag-state (registry country) and class rules.

keyPoints: Marine engineering covers design, operation and maintenance of ship machinery and systems.
Ship types include bulk carriers, tankers, container ships, passenger ships, offshore support vessels and tugs.
The main system produces propulsion; auxiliary systems support it and the ship.
Port is left facing forward, starboard right; forward is towards the bow, aft towards the stern.
The master commands the ship; the chief engineer heads the engine department.
Safety culture uses risk assessment, permits to work, short briefings and stop-work authority; codes and registration differ by country, for example COREN in Nigeria.

en.title: Ship construction and stability fundamentals
en.short: Hull structure, ship geometry, buoyancy, displacement, stability, trim, resistance and propulsion basics.

sections.heading: Hull and geometry
sections.text:
A hull is a stiffened shell. The keel, shell plating, decks and bulkheads form the main structure; frames and longitudinals stiffen the plating. Bulkheads divide the hull into watertight compartments. Classification society rules govern construction and vary by country.

Geometry uses length between perpendiculars L, beam B, draught T and depth D. Freeboard is the height of the freeboard deck above the waterline. Block coefficient Cb = underwater volume ÷ (L × B × T).

sections.heading: Buoyancy and displacement
sections.text:
Buoyancy is the upward force from displaced water. Archimedes’ principle says it equals the weight of water displaced. Displacement mass m = ρ × ∇, where ρ is water density and ∇ is underwater volume. Light displacement is the empty ship. Deadweight is cargo, fuel, water and stores. Loaded displacement is light displacement plus deadweight.

Example: L = 60 m, B = 12 m, T = 3 m, Cb = 0.85, ρ = 1025 kg/m³.
∇ = 0.85 × 60 × 12 × 3 = 1836 m³
m = 1025 × 1836 = 1,881,900 kg = 1881.9 t

sections.heading: Stability and trim
sections.text:
Stability is the tendency to return upright after heel. G is the centre of gravity and B the centre of buoyancy. The metacentre M is the point where the buoyancy force line crosses the ship’s centreline for a small heel; its height depends on hull shape. For small angles, GM = KM − KG, where KM and KG are heights above the keel, and righting lever GZ = GM sin θ. Positive GM means stable, but too large a GM gives a stiff roll. Free liquid surfaces lower effective GM.

Trim is the forward-aft draught difference. Moving a weight along the ship creates a trimming moment equal to weight × distance shifted.

sections.heading: Resistance and propulsion
sections.text:
A moving hull meets resistance from friction, wave making and pressure effects. Friction depends on wetted area and speed. Wave resistance rises with speed. Propulsion overcomes resistance: thrust equals resistance in steady motion. Propulsive efficiency is useful power delivered to the ship divided by power supplied to the propeller.

Example: resistance 40 kN at 5 m/s needs power P = F × v = 40,000 × 5 = 200 kW. If the propeller receives 250 kW, propulsive efficiency is 200 ÷ 250 = 0.80, or 80%.

keyPoints: Block coefficient Cb = underwater volume ÷ (L × B × T).
Displacement mass m = ρ × ∇, where ∇ is underwater volume.
Loaded displacement = light displacement + deadweight.
For small heel, GM = KM − KG and GZ = GM sin θ.
Steady thrust equals resistance, and power P = F × v.
Propulsive efficiency = useful power ÷ power supplied to the propeller.

en.title: Marine diesel engines
en.short: Two-stroke and four-stroke cycles, scavenging, turbocharging, fuel injection, starting, reversing and faults.

sections.heading: Cycles and scavenging
sections.text:
In a four-stroke diesel the piston makes four strokes: intake, compression, power and exhaust. One power stroke occurs every two crankshaft revolutions. In a two-stroke diesel the piston uncovers inlet and exhaust ports near the bottom of the stroke; fresh air from a blower sweeps out exhaust gas and the power stroke occurs every revolution. This sweeping is scavenging. Large marine two-strokes often use uniflow scavenging, with exhaust valves in the head and air ports in the cylinder liner.

Compression ratio r = (swept volume + clearance volume) ÷ clearance volume. Example: bore 300 mm, stroke 600 mm, clearance volume 0.002 m³. Swept volume = π ÷ 4 × 0.3² × 0.6 = 0.0424 m³. r = (0.0424 + 0.002) ÷ 0.002 = 22.2.

sections.heading: Air, fuel and starting
sections.text:
Turbocharging uses exhaust gas to drive a turbine that turns a compressor. The compressor raises the density of the charge air, so more fuel can be burned. A charge-air cooler lowers the air temperature after compression. Fuel injection is by a high-pressure pump and injector; timing and atomisation affect combustion. Large engines may use common-rail injection.

Starting is by compressed air admitted to selected cylinders to turn the engine. Reversing may be done by shifting the camshaft to change valve and injection timing, by a reversing gearbox, or by electric control in modern engines.

sections.heading: Construction, operation and faults
sections.text: The main parts are the bedplate, frame, cylinder block, cylinder head, piston, connecting rod, crankshaft and bearings. Operation needs correct cooling, lubrication and load control. Common faults include worn injectors, poor combustion, fouling of scavenge spaces, scavenge fires, and abnormal bearing wear. Regular inspection and condition monitoring help.

keyPoints: Four-stroke: one power stroke per two revolutions; two-stroke: one per revolution.
Scavenging replaces exhaust gas with fresh air; two-strokes need a blower.
Turbocharging raises charge-air density using exhaust energy.
Compression ratio r = (swept volume + clearance volume) ÷ clearance volume.
Starting air turns the engine; reversing changes valve and injection timing or uses a gearbox.
Common faults include injector wear, poor combustion, scavenge fires and bearing wear.

en.title: Marine boilers and steam systems
en.short: Boiler types, feedwater treatment, combustion, steam distribution, condensate and efficiency.

sections.heading: Boiler types
sections.text: Marine boilers make steam for heating, fuel treatment, tank cleaning and, on steam ships, propulsion. A fire-tube or smoke-tube boiler has hot gas inside tubes surrounded by water; it is compact and suits lower pressures. A water-tube boiler has water inside tubes heated by gas; it suits higher pressures and rapid steam demand. Auxiliary boilers serve hotel and cargo loads. An exhaust gas economiser recovers heat from engine exhaust, often with an oil-fired boiler as backup. The choice depends on pressure, steam rate, space and the ship’s trade; national and classification rules apply, so check the flag state and class society requirements.

sections.heading: Feedwater and combustion
sections.text: Feedwater treatment protects the boiler. Scale-forming salts are removed or controlled, dissolved oxygen is driven off in a deaerator and scavenged by chemicals, and pH and conductivity are held in range. Blowdown removes dissolved solids. Combustion needs atomised fuel, enough air and a stable flame. Too little air gives carbon monoxide and soot; too much wastes heat up the stack. Oxygen trim and flame-failure protection are common.

sections.heading: Steam and condensate
sections.text: Steam leaves the boiler through a main with drains at low points. Pressure-reducing valves supply lower-pressure services. Steam traps remove condensate without losing live steam; failed traps waste energy or cause water hammer. Condensate returns to a hotwell or feed tank. Contamination by oil or salt is tested before return. Insulation and good drainage reduce losses.

sections.heading: Efficiency and safety
sections.text: Boiler efficiency is useful heat output divided by fuel energy input. Example: steam gains 2,000 kW and fuel supplies 2,500 kW, so efficiency = 2,000 ÷ 2,500 = 0.80, or 80%. Stack loss, blowdown and radiation are the main losses. Safety depends on correct water level, tested safety valves, low-water and flame-failure trips, and routine inspection. Rules differ by country and class; follow the current official requirements.

keyPoints: Boiler efficiency = useful heat output ÷ fuel energy input.
Fire-tube boilers suit lower pressures; water-tube boilers suit higher pressures and rapid steam demand.
Feedwater treatment controls scale, oxygen corrosion and carryover by deaeration, chemicals, pH control and blowdown.
Excess air must be controlled: too little causes carbon monoxide and soot, too much lowers efficiency.
Steam traps and drains remove condensate and prevent water hammer.
Safety needs reliable water level, tested safety valves, flame-failure and low-water trips, and inspection under the flag state and class rules.

en.title: Marine steam and gas turbines
en.short: Steam and gas turbine cycles, blading, gearing, combined cycles, operation and faults.

sections.heading: Principles
sections.text: Steam turbines use the Rankine cycle: steam expands through nozzles and blade passages, converting heat energy into shaft work. Gas turbines follow the Brayton cycle: compressor, combustor, turbine. Impulse blading accelerates flow in fixed nozzles and turns it in moving blades; reaction blading also accelerates it in moving blades. Power is P = m × Δh, where m is mass flow and Δh is the specific enthalpy drop (energy per kg). Example: m = 10 kg/s and Δh = 100 kJ/kg give P = 10 × 100 = 1,000 kW = 1 MW. Real output is lower after losses.

sections.heading: Construction and gearing
sections.text: Rotors carry blades in rows; stators and diaphragms guide steam or gas. Casings contain pressure, seals limit leakage, and journal and thrust bearings carry load. Steam turbines run at high speed, so a reduction gearbox lowers shaft speed to the propeller. Gear ratio = turbine speed ÷ shaft speed. Gas turbines may drive through reduction gearing, often with a free power turbine, or through electric transmission. Materials resist creep, fatigue and hot corrosion.

sections.heading: Combined cycles
sections.text: A combined cycle uses gas turbine exhaust heat in a heat recovery steam generator (HRSG) to raise steam for a steam turbine. Efficiency rises because less heat is rejected. Overall efficiency = useful work output ÷ fuel energy input. Example: 30 MW gas turbine and 12 MW steam turbine from 100 MW fuel give (30 + 12) ÷ 100 = 42%. Marine combined gas and steam electric systems exist, but arrangement depends on the ship and operator.

sections.heading: Operation and faults
sections.text: Steam turbine start-up includes warming through, turning gear, gland sealing and draining condensate; gas turbine start-up includes cranking, ignition and acceleration to idle. Monitor vibration, bearing temperature, exhaust temperature spread, lube oil and steam or gas conditions. Common faults are blade erosion, deposits, imbalance, misalignment, bearing failure and compressor surge. Surge is unstable flow with loud pulsation; it can damage blades. Follow the maker’s instructions and classification rules; limits vary by design and country.

keyPoints: Steam turbines use the Rankine cycle and gas turbines use the Brayton cycle.
Turbine power is P = m × Δh, with m in kg/s and Δh in kJ/kg giving kW.
Impulse blading accelerates flow in fixed nozzles; reaction blading also accelerates it in moving blades.
Reduction gearing matches high turbine speed to low propeller speed; gear ratio = turbine speed ÷ shaft speed.
A combined cycle uses gas turbine exhaust in an HRSG to drive a steam turbine; overall efficiency = useful work output ÷ fuel energy input.
Monitor vibration, temperatures, oil and exhaust spread; surge, erosion, deposits and bearing faults are common.

en.title: Ship propulsion: propellers and shafting
en.short: Propeller theory, cavitation, hull interaction, shafting, bearings, stern tubes, gears and alignment.

sections.heading: Propeller theory
sections.text:
Propellers make thrust by accelerating water aft. Pitch is the advance in one turn in a solid medium; slip is the loss between theoretical and actual advance.

The open-water diagram plots thrust coefficient K_T and torque coefficient K_Q against advance coefficient J = V ÷ (nD), where V is speed of advance, n revolutions per second and D diameter. Efficiency η = (J ÷ 2π)(K_T ÷ K_Q).

Example: pitch 4.0 m, n = 2 rev/s, speed through water 6.0 m/s. Theoretical advance per second = 4.0 × 2 = 8.0 m/s, so slip = (8.0 − 6.0) ÷ 8.0 = 25%.

sections.heading: Cavitation and interaction
sections.text:
Cavitation is vapour forming where local pressure falls below vapour pressure, usually near blade tips on the suction face. Bubble collapse erodes blades and causes noise, vibration and thrust loss. Enough blade area, deep immersion and modest loading avoid it; empirical charts such as Burrill’s chart guide the choice of blade area.

The hull slows the water, so speed of advance is V(1 − w), w being the wake fraction, and thrust must exceed resistance: T = R ÷ (1 − t), t being thrust deduction. Hull efficiency is (1 − t) ÷ (1 − w).

sections.heading: Shafting and bearings
sections.text:
The propeller shaft is the aftermost shaft; intermediate shafts connect it to the engine. The stern tube is the housing where the shaft passes through the shell, with bearings and seals keeping sea water out and lubricant in. Bearings are often white metal (babbitt) in oil, or water-lubricated composites. A thrust block, in the gearbox or engine or a separate unit, passes thrust to the hull.

Example: 2.0 MW at 120 rpm gives n = 2 rev/s and torque Q = P ÷ (2πn) = 2,000,000 ÷ 12.57 = 159 kN·m.

sections.heading: Gears and alignment
sections.text: Low-speed two-stroke diesels usually drive fixed-pitch propellers directly; medium-speed engines need reduction gearing, and many ships fit controllable-pitch propellers. Alignment sets the shaft line so bearing loads stay within the builder’s limits, checked by sag and gap readings at flange couplings and rechecked afloat as the hull deflects. Classification societies set the rules; details differ between societies.

keyPoints: Slip = (pitch × n − V) ÷ (pitch × n).
Open-water efficiency η = (J ÷ 2π)(K_T ÷ K_Q).
Cavitation occurs when local pressure falls below vapour pressure; it erodes blades and cuts thrust.
Speed of advance is V(1 − w) and required thrust is R ÷ (1 − t).
Shaft torque Q = P ÷ (2πn), with n in revolutions per second.
The stern tube carries the shaft through the shell; the thrust block passes thrust to the hull.

en.title: Marine pumps, piping and valves
en.short: Pump types, system curves, cavitation, piping, valves, testing and flow control.

sections.heading: Pumps and system curves
sections.text: Marine pumps move seawater, fuel, lubricating oil and other fluids. Centrifugal pumps use a rotating impeller and suit large flows at modest pressure. Positive displacement pumps, such as gear, screw and reciprocating types, trap a fixed volume per cycle and suit high pressure or viscous oil. A pump runs where its head-flow curve meets the system curve, the head needed to overcome static lift and friction. Throttling a discharge valve steepens the system curve and moves the duty point to lower flow.

sections.heading: Cavitation and NPSH
sections.text: Cavitation is vapour bubbles forming and collapsing when local pressure falls below vapour pressure. It causes noise, erosion and head loss. Net positive suction head available (NPSHa) is absolute suction pressure at the pump inlet minus vapour pressure, expressed as head. NPSHa must exceed the maker’s required NPSHr. Example: atmospheric pressure 101 kPa, suction lift 3 m, friction loss 0.5 m, vapour pressure 2.3 kPa, density 1000 kg/m³. NPSHa = (101,000 − 2,300) ÷ (1000 × 9.81) − 3 − 0.5 = 10.06 − 3.5 = 6.56 m.

sections.heading: Piping, valves and fittings
sections.text: Piping layout should be short, supported and free of air pockets. Bends and fittings add friction, so size pipes from a friction-loss calculation and keep velocities reasonable. Valves control or isolate flow: gate valves isolate with low loss, globe valves regulate, butterfly valves save space, and non-return valves prevent backflow. Fittings include elbows, tees, reducers and flanges. Materials must suit the fluid; seawater service needs corrosion-resistant alloys or coatings.

sections.heading: Testing and flow control
sections.text: Pressure testing proves joints and pipework before service. Hydrostatic testing fills the system with water and pressurises it above design pressure; pneumatic testing uses air but stores more energy and is more dangerous. Test pressure and duration follow the applicable national or classification society rule, so check the current rule. Flow control uses valve position, pump speed or a bypass. Variable-speed drives save energy by matching speed to demand; affinity laws show flow varies with speed and head with speed squared.

keyPoints: Centrifugal pumps suit high flow, while positive displacement pumps suit high pressure or viscous fluids.
A pump’s duty point is where the pump curve meets the system curve.
NPSHa = (p − pv) ÷ (ρg) − suction lift − suction friction, and it must exceed NPSHr.
Cavitation causes noise, erosion and head loss.
Pressure tests must follow the applicable national or classification society rule.
Flow can be controlled by throttling, pump speed or a bypass; affinity laws relate flow and head to speed.

en.title: Marine auxiliary machinery
en.short: Air compressors, separators, heat exchangers, steering gear, deck machinery and fresh water systems.

sections.heading: Air and oil
sections.text: Compressed air starts engines and drives tools and controls. A ship service air compressor draws through filters, compresses in stages with intercoolers, and delivers to receivers. Intercoolers reduce air temperature and water is drained from traps. Safety valves, unloaders and pressure switches protect the system. Fuel and lube oil separators are centrifugal purifiers: they spin oil so water and solids move outward and are removed. Correct temperature and flow matter; check maker instructions.

sections.heading: Heat exchange
sections.text: Heat exchangers move heat between fluids without mixing them. Shell-and-tube and plate types are common. The log mean temperature difference (LMTD) drives heat flow; for counter-flow, LMTD = (dT1 − dT2) ÷ ln(dT1 ÷ dT2). Q = U × A × LMTD, where U is overall heat transfer coefficient and A area. Fouling raises resistance, so clean and vent. Example: hot oil 90 to 60 °C, cooling water 25 to 45 °C. dT1 = 45 K, dT2 = 35 K, LMTD = 10 ÷ ln(45÷35) = 39.8 K. With Q = 120 kW and U = 500 W/m²K, A = 120000 ÷ (500 × 39.8) = 6.03 m².

sections.heading: Steering and deck
sections.text: Steering gear turns the rudder. Electro-hydraulic systems use pumps, rams or rotary vanes, and follow-up control so the rudder angle matches the helm. SOLAS (International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea) and class rules require emergency steering and drills; exact rules depend on flag state. Deck machinery includes windlass, mooring winches and capstans. Brakes, clutches, guards and remote controls need routine checks, and operators must avoid overloading wires and drums.

sections.heading: Fresh water
sections.text: Fresh water generators make distilled water by evaporating seawater under vacuum using waste engine heat. Reverse osmosis is an alternative. Distilled water is low in minerals, so potable supplies are mineralised and disinfected, often by chlorination or UV. Tanks, filters and sampling protect quality. Check local potable water rules and the maker’s instructions.

keyPoints: Compressors are staged with intercoolers; drain traps and safety devices protect the system.
Centrifugal separators remove water and solids from fuel and lube oil; follow maker settings.
Heat exchanger duty: Q = U × A × LMTD; fouling adds resistance.
Steering gear is usually electro-hydraulic with follow-up control; SOLAS and class rules apply, with national differences.
Deck machinery such as windlass and winches needs brake, clutch and wire checks.
Fresh water generators use waste heat under vacuum; potable water needs mineralisation and disinfection.

en.title: Marine electrical power systems
en.short: Generation, distribution, switchboards, protection, earthing, emergency power, shore supply and safety.

sections.heading: Generation and distribution
sections.text: Ship generators are usually diesel-driven or shaft-driven alternators producing three-phase AC. Frequency is 50 or 60 Hz and voltage depends on ship design and flag/class rules, so check the vessel’s documentation. Generated power goes to the main switchboard, then feeders and distribution boards. Essential loads, such as steering gear and fire pumps, are kept separate from non-essential loads so that non-essential load can be shed first when the supply is overloaded. A busbar is a common conductor linking generators and feeders.

sections.heading: Switchboards and protection
sections.text: Switchboards carry busbars, circuit breakers, fuses, meters and interlocks. Protection must clear a fault quickly and only the nearest breaker should trip, which is discrimination. Typical protections include overcurrent, short circuit, earth fault, reverse power, under-voltage and under-frequency. Earth fault monitoring matters because many marine systems use an insulated neutral, not a direct connection to the hull; the hull is the common earth reference.

sections.heading: Emergency power and shore supply
sections.text: An emergency generator or battery bank supplies the emergency switchboard if the main supply fails. It starts automatically and feeds safety loads such as emergency lighting, alarms and radio. Shore supply connects the ship to land power through a matched cable and switchgear. Before closing, check voltage, frequency, phase sequence and earthing, and use an interlock so ship and shore supplies cannot be connected together.

sections.heading: Example and safety
sections.text: Example: a 150 kW three-phase load at 400 V and power factor 0.8 draws I = P ÷ (√3 × V × cos φ) = 150,000 ÷ (1.732 × 400 × 0.8) = 271 A. Its apparent power is 150 ÷ 0.8 = 187.5 kVA. Electrical safety means isolating and proving dead before work, using lockout/tagout, insulated tools and personal protective equipment (PPE), and treating wet or hot spaces as high risk.

keyPoints: Three-phase power: P = √3 × V × I × cos φ, so I = P ÷ (√3 × V × cos φ).
Apparent power S = P ÷ cos φ.
Marine systems often use an insulated neutral with earth fault monitoring; the hull is the earth reference.
Protection must be selective: the nearest breaker clears the fault.
Emergency power starts automatically and feeds safety loads.
Shore supply needs matching voltage, frequency and phase sequence, plus an interlock and earthing check.

en.title: Marine automation, instrumentation and control
en.short: Sensors, transmitters, PID loops, alarms and engine room automation on ships.

sections.heading: Sensing and signals
sections.text: Marine instruments measure temperature, pressure, level, flow and speed. A sensor produces a small electrical or mechanical signal. A transmitter converts it into a standard signal, commonly 4-20 mA, sent along a current loop. In a 4-20 mA loop, 4 mA represents the lower end of the range and 20 mA the upper end. A current near 0 mA can show a broken wire, so the live zero helps fault detection. Digital fieldbus links are also used. Instruments need calibration against a known reference; drift and vibration cause errors.

sections.heading: PID control
sections.text:
A control loop compares the measured value with the setpoint. The error is setpoint minus measurement. The controller drives an actuator, such as a valve or fuel rack, to reduce the error. In proportional control, output change = Kp × error. Integral action removes steady offset. Derivative action responds to rate of change and can amplify noise. The combined PID output is proportional plus integral plus derivative contributions, added to a bias.

Example: error = 2 °C, Kp = 4 %/°C, integral contribution = 3 %, derivative contribution = −1 %, bias = 50 %. Output = 50 + (4 × 2) + 3 − 1 = 60 %. Tuning must suit the process; too much gain causes cycling.

sections.heading: Alarms and automation
sections.text: Alarms warn when a value passes a setpoint. A deadband prevents chattering near the limit, and a time delay avoids alarms from short spikes. Priority separates critical from advisory alarms. First-out alarm recording shows the first cause in a trip sequence. Engine room automation uses programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and monitoring systems to start pumps, control temperature and shut down engines. Remote monitoring sends data to the bridge or shore. Safety functions should fail safe, and changes need testing and records. Classification societies and flag states set requirements; these vary by country and ship.

keyPoints: A transmitter converts a sensor signal into a standard signal, often 4-20 mA.
Control error = setpoint − measured value.
PID output = bias + Kp × error + integral term + derivative term.
Integral action removes steady offset; derivative action responds to rate of change.
Alarm deadband and delay reduce nuisance alarms.
Engine room automation uses PLCs and monitoring; safety functions should fail safe and be tested.

en.title: Marine refrigeration and air conditioning
en.short: Vapour compression cycles, refrigerants, components, psychrometry, cold rooms, HVAC and safety.

sections.heading: Vapour compression cycle
sections.text:
Marine refrigeration removes heat from a cold space and rejects it to sea water or air. In the vapour compression cycle, the evaporator absorbs heat at low pressure, the compressor raises the vapour pressure and temperature, the condenser rejects heat, and the expansion device drops the pressure. COP = refrigeration effect ÷ compressor work, or (h1 − h4) ÷ (h2 − h1) using enthalpies.

Example: h1 = 400 kJ/kg, h2 = 450 kJ/kg and h4 = 250 kJ/kg. COP = (400 − 250) ÷ (450 − 400) = 150 ÷ 50 = 3.0. Actual COP is lower.

sections.heading: Components and refrigerants
sections.text:
The main components are compressor, condenser, evaporator and expansion valve, with receiver, oil separator, filters, controls and safety devices. Refrigerants include ammonia (R717), carbon dioxide (R744), hydrocarbons and HFCs such as R134a. Ammonia is efficient but toxic; hydrocarbons are flammable; carbon dioxide works at high pressure. HFCs have high global warming potential and are being phased down under the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol, while national rules differ.

Refrigerant handling needs recovery, ventilation, leak detection and protective equipment. Never mix refrigerants or charge a system without checking its design.

sections.heading: Psychrometry and cold rooms
sections.text: Psychrometry is the study of moist air. It uses dry-bulb temperature, humidity ratio, relative humidity, dew point and enthalpy. A cooling coil below the dew point condenses water and dehumidifies the air. Cold rooms need insulation, a vapour barrier, tight doors, air curtains, defrost, drainage and temperature control. The cooling load includes heat through walls, product load, infiltration and internal heat from lights, fans and people.

sections.heading: HVAC and safety
sections.text:
Marine HVAC conditions accommodation air by heating, cooling, humidifying, dehumidifying, filtering and distributing it through ducts and fans. Design codes, refrigerant rules and registration requirements differ by country and classification society, so check current flag State and class requirements.

Safety covers pressure relief, electrical isolation, refrigerant detection, ventilation, fire dampers and ammonia plant procedures. Only trained personnel should work on refrigerant circuits.

keyPoints: COP = refrigeration effect ÷ compressor work, or (h1 − h4) ÷ (h2 − h1) using enthalpies.
The vapour compression cycle has evaporation, compression, condensation and expansion.
Ammonia is efficient but toxic; hydrocarbons are flammable; carbon dioxide operates at high pressure.
Psychrometry uses dry-bulb temperature, humidity ratio, relative humidity, dew point and enthalpy.
Cold-room loads include transmission, product, infiltration and internal heat.
Refrigerant and HVAC work requires recovery, ventilation, leak detection and checks against flag State and class rules.

en.title: Marine fuels, lubricants and combustion
en.short: Fuel properties, onboard treatment, combustion, lubricants and oil analysis.

sections.heading: Fuel properties
sections.text:
Marine fuels range from distillates to residual fuel oils. Key properties include density, viscosity, flash point, pour point, sulphur, water, ash, vanadium and calorific value.

Viscosity affects pumping and atomisation; it is measured at a stated temperature and corrected to a reference temperature. Cetane number describes ignition quality of distillates. ISO 8217 is the international standard for marine fuel quality; it sets test methods and limits, which you should check in the current edition. Fuel stability and compatibility matter when blending, because asphaltenes (heavy fuel components) can precipitate and block filters.

sections.heading: Onboard treatment
sections.text:
Fuel is stored, settled, heated, centrifuged and filtered before burning. Settling tanks let water and sludge separate by gravity.

Heaters reduce viscosity so centrifuges and burners work. Purifiers remove water and solids; filters catch remaining particles. Additives may improve stability or combustion, but they do not correct badly contaminated fuel. Treatment must match the fuel; a residual fuel needs more heating than a distillate.

sections.heading: Combustion
sections.text:
Combustion is the rapid reaction of fuel with oxygen, releasing heat. In a diesel engine, fuel is atomised, evaporates, mixes with air and ignites. Complete combustion needs enough air and time. The excess air ratio, lambda, is the actual air divided by the stoichiometric air. Stoichiometric air is the theoretical air needed for complete combustion; it can be estimated from fuel composition.

Example: 1 kg fuel with 86% C, 12% H2 and 2% S. Oxygen: C: 0.86 × 32/12 = 2.293 kg; H2: 0.12 × 16/2 = 0.960 kg; S: 0.02 × 32/32 = 0.020 kg. Total O2 = 3.273 kg. Air is 23.2% O2 by mass, so stoichiometric air = 3.273 ÷ 0.232 = 14.1 kg per kg fuel. Lambda = actual air ÷ 14.1.

sections.heading: Lubricants and oil analysis
sections.text:
Lubricating oil reduces friction, removes heat and carries wear particles. It is base oil plus additives: detergents, dispersants, anti-wear and corrosion inhibitors.

Total base number (TBN) measures acid neutralising capacity. Oil analysis tracks viscosity, water, insolubles, TBN and wear metals. Trends matter more than single results. Follow the engine maker’s guidance.

keyPoints: Marine fuel quality is described by properties such as density, viscosity, sulphur, water and stability; ISO 8217 is the international standard, but check the current edition.
Onboard treatment uses settling, heating, centrifugation and filtration to remove water and solids before combustion.
Stoichiometric oxygen for 1 kg fuel is O2 = 2.667C + 8H + S, with C, H and S as mass fractions.
Stoichiometric air is about O2 ÷ 0.232; lambda is actual air ÷ stoichiometric air.
Lubricant TBN measures acid neutralising capacity, and oil analysis trends show contamination and wear.
Fuel sulphur and engine design affect lubricant choice; follow the engine maker’s guidance.

en.title: Corrosion and material protection
en.short: Corrosion mechanisms, coatings, cathodic protection, inhibitors, material selection and inspection.

sections.heading: Corrosion mechanisms
sections.text:
Corrosion is electrochemical. Metal dissolves at an anode, releasing electrons that travel through the metal to a cathode, where oxygen or hydrogen ions are reduced. Seawater conducts because it contains dissolved salts, mainly sodium and chloride ions. Dissolved oxygen in the water takes part in the cathodic reaction. The galvanic series ranks metals by potential; joining dissimilar metals in seawater makes the less noble one the anode and speeds its loss.

Forms include uniform thinning, pitting, crevice attack, galvanic corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, corrosion fatigue and erosion-corrosion. Trapped water and sharp corners raise the rate.

sections.heading: Coatings and cathodic protection
sections.text:
Coatings are the first barrier. Abrasive blasting and the correct primer and topcoat keep water and oxygen from steel. The system depends on the area: hull, ballast tank or deck. Repair damage promptly.

Cathodic protection makes the structure the cathode. Sacrificial anodes of zinc or aluminium alloy dissolve instead of steel. Impressed current systems use an external supply and inert anodes. CP works with coatings; bare steel needs much more current. Protection criteria and anode life come from classification society rules and flag State requirements, so check the current edition.

sections.heading: Inhibitors, materials, inspection
sections.text:
Inhibitors are chemicals added in small amounts to closed systems. Anodic inhibitors film the anode, cathodic inhibitors slow the cathode, and mixed inhibitors do both. They are not practical for an open hull.

Material selection avoids trouble at design. Carbon steel with a corrosion allowance (extra thickness) is common; stainless steels, copper-nickel, titanium and composites suit particular services. Avoid dissimilar joints or isolate them.

Inspection uses visual survey, coating checks and ultrasonic thickness measurement. Coupons and probes monitor rate. Classification societies set survey intervals and acceptance limits; these vary, so use the rules for your ship and flag State.

Example: a plate was 12.0 mm and is now 10.4 mm after 4 years.
Loss = 1.6 mm, rate = 1.6 ÷ 4 = 0.4 mm/year.
If minimum allowed is 9.0 mm, remaining life = (10.4 − 9.0) ÷ 0.4 = 3.5 years.
Actual limits come from the rules.

keyPoints: Corrosion is electrochemical: an anode dissolves, electrons flow to a cathode, and seawater acts as the electrolyte.
Coatings are the main barrier; cathodic protection makes the structure the cathode using sacrificial anodes or impressed current.
Inhibitors suit closed systems, not open hulls; material selection and good design reduce corrosion.
Corrosion rate = thickness loss ÷ time; ultrasonic thickness measurement finds the loss.
Classification societies and flag States set survey intervals and acceptance limits, and these vary by country and ship.
Avoid dissimilar metal joints in seawater, or isolate them, because the less noble metal becomes the anode.

en.title: Maintenance and condition monitoring
en.short: Planned and breakdown maintenance, condition monitoring by vibration, oil and thermography, spares and reliability.

sections.heading: Maintenance strategies
sections.text:
Planned maintenance is work scheduled before failure. It includes preventive work at fixed intervals, predictive work triggered by condition data, and planned repair after a defect is found. Breakdown maintenance repairs only after failure; it suits cheap, non-critical items whose failure is safe and does not stop the ship.

A planned maintenance system (PMS) records jobs, intervals and history. Intervals come from the manufacturer, operator experience and class or flag requirements. These differ by country and ship, so use approved documentation.

sections.heading: Condition monitoring
sections.text:
Condition monitoring measures machine health. Vibration analysis measures velocity or acceleration with sensors; a rising trend or bearing tones can point to misalignment, imbalance, looseness or bearing damage. Oil analysis checks lubricant samples for wear metals, water, viscosity, acidity and particles against a baseline. Thermography uses an infrared camera to find hot bearings, joints and electrical connections.

Use trends, not one reading. Example: pump bearing vibration rises from 2.0 to 4.5 mm/s over weeks. That justifies checking alignment, lubrication and bearing condition before failure. Alarm limits come from the manufacturer or applicable standard.

sections.heading: Spares and reliability
sections.text:
Reliability is the probability that an item performs its required function under stated conditions for a stated time. The bathtub curve shows early failures, random failures in useful life, then wear-out. Mean time between failures (MTBF) is total operating time divided by the number of failures. Mean time to repair (MTTR) is average repair time. Availability A = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR).

Worked example: MTBF = 2,000 h and MTTR = 100 h.
A = 2,000 ÷ (2,000 + 100) = 2,000 ÷ 2,100 = 0.952 (95.2%).

Spares policy balances holding cost against downtime risk. Stock critical items first: long lead times, no redundancy, and safety or propulsion impact. Protect stores from corrosion and record shelf life. A Lagos ferry operator might hold a sea-water pump impeller set, but wait for breakdown on cheap deck fittings.

keyPoints: Planned maintenance includes preventive, predictive and planned repair work; breakdown maintenance is run to failure.
Vibration, oil and thermography readings are judged by trend against a baseline, not by one reading.
Reliability is the probability of performing a required function under stated conditions for a stated time.
Availability A = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR), where MTBF is mean time between failures and MTTR is mean time to repair.
Spares should be stocked by criticality, lead time, redundancy and safety impact.
Maintenance intervals and condition limits come from manufacturer, operator and class or flag requirements, which vary by country and ship.

en.title: Ship safety, fire protection and life-saving
en.short: Fire triangle, detection, suppression, structural protection, life-saving appliances, drills and SOLAS.

sections.heading: Fire and detection
sections.text:
Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat together, shown as the fire triangle. Remove one and combustion stops. The fire tetrahedron adds the chemical chain reaction. On board, fuel may be oil, paint or cargo; oxygen comes from air; heat comes from exhausts, electrical faults or hot work.

Detection gives early warning. Smoke detectors suit accommodation, heat detectors suit galleys and machinery, and flame detectors suit fuel-handling spaces. Alarms must reach a manned control point. Testing and clear escape routes matter as much as detector type.

sections.heading: Suppression and structure
sections.text:
Suppression removes heat, oxygen or fuel, or interrupts the chain reaction. Portable extinguishers handle small fires; fixed systems protect machinery, galleys and cargo holds. Water cools but conducts electricity; foam blankets liquid fuel; carbon dioxide displaces oxygen; dry powder interrupts the chain reaction. Before releasing carbon dioxide into a machinery space, seal it and account for all personnel.

Structural fire protection divides the ship into zones with fire-resisting boundaries, restricts combustibles and protects escape routes. Openings and ducts must not defeat these boundaries. Case: a fuel leak sprays onto a hot exhaust. Detection alarms, fuel is isolated, ventilation stopped, boundary cooling starts, and the fixed system is released only after sealing and head count.

sections.heading: Life-saving and drills
sections.text: Life-saving appliances include lifebuoys, lifejackets, immersion suits, lifeboats, rescue boats, liferafts, launching appliances, EPIRBs (emergency position-indicating radio beacons), SARTs (search and rescue radar transponders) and pyrotechnics. They must be approved, stowed, marked and maintained. Drills practise muster, roles, launching and abandon-ship procedures, and are recorded. Intervals and equipment details are set by SOLAS and flag-state rules; check current requirements.

sections.heading: Risk and SOLAS
sections.text: Risk assessment identifies hazards, estimates likelihood and severity, and sets controls: eliminate, substitute, engineer, administrate, then use PPE. Review after changes or near misses. SOLAS, the IMO ship safety convention, sets principles: divide the ship into fire zones, restrict combustibles, detect and contain fire near its origin, protect escape routes and keep extinguishing appliances ready. Classification societies and flag states enforce it; national rules differ.

keyPoints: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat; removing one stops combustion.
Detection should give early warning and reach a manned control point.
Fixed suppression must match the fire type; seal a machinery space and account for personnel before carbon dioxide release.
Structural fire protection uses fire-resisting boundaries, restricted combustibles and protected escape routes.
Life-saving appliances must be approved, stowed, marked, maintained and practised in drills.
SOLAS principles and flag-state rules set the framework; check current national and IMO requirements.

en.title: Maritime environmental protection
en.short: Pollution sources, MARPOL annexes, oily water, sewage, garbage, air emissions and ballast water.

sections.heading: Pollution sources
sections.text: Ships pollute at sea and in port. Main sources are machinery spaces (fuel, lubricating oil and bilge water), sewage, food and domestic waste, exhaust gases from engines and boilers, cargo residues and cleaning agents, and ballast water carried between ports. Accidental spills and anti-fouling paint also matter. Pollution may be operational or accidental. International rules aim to prevent both.

sections.heading: MARPOL and oily water
sections.text: MARPOL is the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, adopted through the International Maritime Organization (IMO). It has six technical annexes: oil, noxious liquid substances, packaged harmful substances, sewage, garbage and air pollution. Annex I controls oily water. An oily water separator removes oil from bilge water; discharge is allowed only under the annex conditions. The usual international limit is 15 parts per million (ppm) of oil, but check the current text and flag State rules.

sections.heading: Sewage, garbage, air
sections.text: Sewage is covered by Annex IV; treatment plants or holding tanks are used, especially in coastal waters. Garbage is covered by Annex V, which bans the overboard discharge of plastics and requires a garbage management plan and record book on larger ships. Annex VI limits air emissions, including sulphur oxides, nitrogen oxides and ozone-depleting substances, and sets energy efficiency requirements. Exact limits and dates change, so consult the current annex and your flag State.

sections.heading: Ballast water and waste
sections.text: Ballast water is not part of MARPOL. The Ballast Water Management Convention requires ships to manage ballast so that harmful aquatic organisms are not moved between ports. Methods include exchange and treatment; ports also provide reception facilities for sediments. Waste management on board means segregation, labelled bins, storage, landing ashore and record keeping. In a case in Lagos, Nigeria, a crew might separate oily rags, food waste and plastics, keep a garbage record book, and land waste at an approved facility; NIMASA (the Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency), as port State, can inspect. Rules differ by country, so check local requirements.

keyPoints: MARPOL is the IMO convention with six annexes covering oil, noxious liquids, packaged harmful substances, sewage, garbage and air pollution.
Oily bilge water is treated with an oily water separator; the usual international discharge limit is 15 ppm, but confirm current rules.
Sewage and garbage are controlled by MARPOL Annex IV and Annex V; plastics are banned from overboard disposal.
MARPOL Annex VI controls air emissions such as sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides; limits change over time.
Ballast water is governed by the separate Ballast Water Management Convention, not MARPOL.
Good waste management means segregation, labelled storage, landing ashore at approved facilities and keeping records.

en.title: Maritime law, classification and certification
en.short: Flag and port state control, IMO rules, class societies, surveys, certificates and insurance.

sections.heading: Flag and port state
sections.text: A ship must fly the flag of one state. That flag state has jurisdiction over the ship and must enforce the international rules it has accepted, mainly IMO instruments: SOLAS for safety, MARPOL for pollution, STCW for crew training and COLREG for collision avoidance. The flag state issues certificates, often through recognised organisations. Port state control is inspection of foreign ships in a state’s ports by that state’s officers. They check certificates and condition; serious deficiencies can lead to detention until repaired. Regional agreements coordinate inspections, such as the Abuja MoU in West and Central Africa.

sections.heading: Classification and surveys
sections.text:
Classification societies are private technical bodies. They publish rules for hull strength, machinery, electrical systems and equipment, survey a ship against those rules and issue a class certificate. IACS is an association of major societies. Class is not the same as statutory certification, but flag states often delegate statutory surveys to recognised organisations, including class societies. Surveys verify that the ship still complies. Class surveys are periodic; statutory surveys support certificates such as load line, safety construction and pollution prevention. Failure can suspend class or a certificate.

Case: a tanker owned by a Lagos company is inspected in port. Her class certificate is valid, but the port state finds a defective fire pump. She may be detained until repaired, even though class has not yet been withdrawn.

sections.heading: Certificates and insurance
sections.text: Certificates are documents showing compliance. Examples are the International Load Line Certificate, Safety Construction Certificate, Safety Equipment Certificate and International Oil Pollution Prevention Certificate. They are issued after survey and kept on board for inspection. Insurance transfers risk. Hull and machinery insurance covers damage to the ship; protection and indemnity (P&I) insurance covers third-party liabilities such as crew injury, pollution and cargo claims. War and cargo policies cover other risks. Marine insurance rests on insurable interest, utmost good faith and indemnity, meaning the insured is restored, not enriched.

keyPoints: Flag state has jurisdiction and enforces IMO instruments for its ships.
Port state control inspects foreign ships and can detain for serious deficiencies.
IMO instruments include SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW and COLREG.
Classification societies set technical rules and issue class certificates; class is not statutory certification.
Surveys verify compliance and support class and statutory certificates.
Hull and machinery covers the ship; P&I covers third-party liabilities.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and regulation
en.short: Engineering ethics, codes of conduct, registration, COREN and other national bodies, CPD and responsibility.

sections.heading: Ethics and codes
sections.text:
Engineering ethics is the study of what an engineer ought to do when duties to the public, an employer, colleagues and the environment conflict. It is not only about avoiding dishonesty. It also asks who may be harmed by a decision and who should bear the risk.

A code of conduct is a written set of rules that a professional body or regulator expects members to follow. Codes differ in detail, but common duties include competence, honesty, confidentiality, avoiding conflicts of interest, keeping public safety and the environment foremost, and reporting genuine concerns. Breach can lead to discipline by an employer or a professional body.

sections.heading: Registration and regulation
sections.text:
Registration is the official recognition of an engineer by a statutory body. It is country-specific. In Nigeria, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN) registers engineers and regulates engineering practice. Requirements, protected titles and penalties differ, so check COREN’s current rules.

Other countries have their own arrangements. Examples include the Engineering Council in the UK, ECSA in South Africa, the Engineers Board of Kenya and state licensing boards in the US. Professional bodies such as IMarEST support marine engineers, but membership of a body is not the same as statutory registration.

sections.heading: CPD and responsibility
sections.text:
Continuing professional development (CPD) is planned learning after qualification: courses, conferences, reading, supervised practice or teaching. It keeps competence current. The required hours, records and audit rules vary by body and country.

Professional responsibility means working within your competence, signing only work you can justify, keeping records, and putting safety before commercial pressure. Case: Ngozi, a graduate engineer in Port Harcourt, finds a sea-water line tested below its specification. Her supervisor asks her to sign the record as satisfactory. She should not sign. She should record the shortfall, report it in writing, and escalate it if the company does not correct it.

keyPoints: Engineering ethics puts public safety, health and the environment ahead of commercial pressure.
A code of conduct sets expected behaviour, and a breach can lead to discipline.
Statutory registration is country-specific; in Nigeria it is through COREN.
Membership of a professional body is not the same as statutory registration.
CPD is planned lifelong learning that keeps competence current; requirements vary.
Sign only work you are competent to certify, keep records, and report unresolved safety concerns.

en.title: Research methods and the final-year project
en.short: Framing a project, reviewing literature, choosing methods, analysing data, ethics and reporting.

sections.heading: Problem and literature
sections.text:
A final-year project starts with a problem, not a topic. Write a problem statement: one or two sentences naming the gap, the system affected and why it matters. In marine engineering the system may be a pump, a hull coating or a fuel line. Then set aims and measurable objectives.

A literature review is a critical summary of what is already known. Use journals, conference papers, textbooks, classification society guidance and manufacturer data. For each source record the method, result and limitation. End with the gap your project addresses. Do not copy; cite every source.

sections.heading: Methods and data
sections.text:
Choose an experimental or computational method that can answer the objective. Experimental work uses physical tests, such as a pipe-flow rig. Computational work uses models, such as a spreadsheet or CFD (computational fluid dynamics). State assumptions, instruments, calibration and uncertainty. A control test or repeat run helps show reliability.

Data analysis turns readings into evidence. For a small sample, report the mean and the spread. Example: four pump pressures in bar are 4.8, 5.0, 4.9 and 5.3. Mean = (4.8 + 5.0 + 4.9 + 5.3) ÷ 4 = 20.0 ÷ 4 = 5.0 bar. Range = 5.3 − 4.8 = 0.5 bar. If the sample is larger, use standard deviation; check whether a trend is real or within instrument error.

sections.heading: Ethics and reporting
sections.text:
Research ethics means honesty and safety. Do not fabricate or alter data. Acknowledge help, keep raw records, obtain permission for tests and follow your institution’s rules. In Nigeria, professional registration is through COREN; other countries have their own bodies. Codes and standards differ by country, so cite the edition you used.

The report usually has title, abstract, introduction, literature review, method, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Write in plain past tense for what you did. Figures need captions and units. The presentation is a short talk: state the problem, method, key result and limitation. Rehearse to time and answer questions with evidence.

keyPoints: A project begins with a clear problem statement, aim and measurable objectives.
A literature review records the method, result and limitation of each source and ends with the gap.
Experimental and computational methods must state assumptions, calibration and uncertainty.
Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values; range = largest value − smallest value.
Never fabricate or alter data; keep raw records and cite the standard edition used.
The report and talk should state problem, method, key result and limitation plainly.

en.title: Advanced marine thermodynamics and energy systems
en.short: Exergy, advanced cycles, waste heat recovery, heat exchanger design and ship energy efficiency.

sections.heading: Exergy
sections.text:
Exergy is the maximum useful work a stream or system can give as it reaches equilibrium with a reference environment, the dead state. Unlike energy, exergy is destroyed by irreversibility.
