The Gouy-Stodola relation is X_destroyed = T0 S_gen, where T0 is dead-state temperature and S_gen is entropy generation. Second-law efficiency compares actual performance with the reversible limit.

Example: 1 kg/s of exhaust gas cools from 500 °C to 150 °C, cp = 1.05 kJ/(kg K), T0 = 25 °C. Heat released is 1.05 × (500 − 150) = 367.5 kW. Flow exergy drop is m cp[(T1 − T2) − T0 ln(T1/T2)] with absolute temperatures: 1 × 1.05 × [(773.15 − 423.15) − 298.15 ln(773.15/423.15)] = 178.8 kW. Much of the heat is low-grade.

sections.heading: Power cycles
sections.text: Advanced marine power cycles aim to raise mean heat-addition temperature and lower rejection temperature. Reheat and regenerative Rankine cycles improve steam plant efficiency. Combined cycles use a gas turbine Brayton cycle and a steam Rankine cycle, recovering gas-turbine exhaust heat. Organic Rankine cycles use a low-boiling working fluid for low-grade waste heat. Cycle analysis uses steady-flow energy balances and the second law; pinch points limit heat recovery.

sections.heading: Heat recovery
sections.text: Waste heat recovery uses exhaust gas economisers, exhaust gas boilers, power turbines, turbo-compounding and absorption chillers. Heat exchanger design must balance duty, pressure drop, fouling and weight. The log-mean temperature difference method gives Q = U A ΔT_lm F, where U is overall coefficient, A area and F a correction factor. The effectiveness-NTU method is better when outlet temperatures are unknown. Bypass control keeps metal temperatures above the acid dew point to limit cold-end corrosion, while fouling margins allow for deposit build-up over time.

sections.heading: Ship efficiency
sections.text: Ship energy efficiency combines thermodynamic performance with operational measures: hull and propeller cleaning, speed management, trim optimisation, waste heat recovery and improved controls. The IMO has adopted measures such as EEDI, EEXI, CII and SEEMP; their details and national enforcement change, so check the current IMO and flag-state requirements. Energy audits should use measured fuel and power data, not nameplate values.

keyPoints: Exergy is maximum useful work to the dead state; X_destroyed = T0 S_gen.
For an ideal gas, flow exergy drop is m cp[(T1 − T2) − T0 ln(T1/T2)].
Reheat, regeneration and combined cycles improve efficiency by better temperature matching.
Waste heat recovery is limited by pinch, fouling and pressure drop.
Heat exchanger duty is Q = U A ΔT_lm F; effectiveness-NTU helps when outlet temperatures are unknown.
IMO efficiency rules and flag-state requirements change, so check current official sources.

en.title: Computational fluid dynamics for marine engineering
en.short: Covers governing equations, turbulence models, meshing, boundary conditions, verification and validation, and marine CFD applications.

sections.heading: Governing equations
sections.text: CFD solves the conservation laws on a grid. For an incompressible fluid, mass conservation is div u = 0. Momentum conservation is the Navier-Stokes equation: ρ(∂u/∂t + u·∇u) = −∇p + μ∇²u + f, where u is velocity, p is pressure, ρ is density, μ is viscosity and f is body force per unit volume. Add the energy equation when heat transfer matters. They have no general analytical solution for ship flows, so they are discretised, usually by the finite volume method: the domain is split into cells and fluxes through cell faces are balanced.

sections.heading: Turbulence and meshing
sections.text: Most marine flows are turbulent. Direct numerical simulation (DNS) resolves every eddy and is far too costly. Large eddy simulation (LES) resolves large eddies and models small ones, expensive. Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) models time-averaged flow; common models are k-epsilon and k-omega SST. RANS is usual for hull and propeller design. Meshing must resolve the boundary layer: y+ is a dimensionless wall distance for the first cell height, and wall functions or low-Re treatment are chosen to suit it. Grid independence repeats runs on finer meshes until results change little.

sections.heading: Boundary and checking
sections.text: Boundary conditions set the flow at domain edges: velocity inlet, pressure outlet, no-slip wall, symmetry plane, and moving wall or rotating frame for propellers. Verification checks numerical error by mesh and time-step refinement and analytical cases. Validation compares predictions with experimental data, such as towing-tank resistance or propeller open-water tests. Example: Courant number C = UΔt ÷ Δx. With U = 2 m/s, Δt = 0.01 s and Δx = 0.1 m, C = 2 × 0.01 ÷ 0.1 = 0.2. Limits depend on the solver and scheme.

sections.heading: Marine applications
sections.text: Hull CFD predicts resistance, pressure distribution and wake. Propeller CFD predicts thrust, torque, open-water efficiency and cavitation risk; rotating frames or sliding meshes handle rotation. Machinery CFD covers cooling-water flow, combustion air, ventilation and heat transfer in engine rooms. Results guide design only after verification and validation; full-scale prediction remains uncertain.

keyPoints: Mass conservation for incompressible flow is div u = 0, and momentum conservation is the Navier-Stokes equation.
RANS is the usual turbulence approach for hull and propeller design; LES and DNS are more costly.
y+ sets the near-wall mesh treatment, and grid independence must be checked.
Boundary conditions include velocity inlet, pressure outlet, no-slip wall and rotating or moving walls.
Verification checks numerical error; validation compares CFD with experiment.
Courant number C = UΔt ÷ Δx; with U = 2 m/s, Δt = 0.01 s and Δx = 0.1 m, C = 0.2.

en.title: Alternative fuels and decarbonisation of shipping
en.short: LNG, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen, batteries, fuel cells, life-cycle emissions, safety and rules.

sections.heading: Fuel options
sections.text:
Alternative fuels are compared by energy per mass and volume, availability, cost and emissions. LNG is mainly methane, stored cryogenically near −162 °C. It cuts CO2, SOx and particulates but can leak methane, a strong greenhouse gas. Methanol is a liquid alcohol, easier to store; it can be fossil or made from renewable hydrogen and captured CO2 (green methanol). Ammonia has no carbon but is toxic. Hydrogen has high energy per mass and low energy per volume, so storage is hard. Batteries suit short voyages and hybrids; fuel cells convert chemical energy directly to electricity.

Example: 1 t of heavy fuel oil gives about 40.5 GJ (lower heating value, LHV, 40.5 MJ/kg). Approximate LHVs give LNG 0.81 t, methanol 2.04 t, ammonia 2.18 t, hydrogen 0.34 t. Tank and engine losses differ.

sections.heading: Life-cycle emissions
sections.text: Life-cycle or well-to-wake emissions count extraction, production, transport, bunkering and use. Tank-to-wake counts only exhaust. A fuel is low-carbon only if its whole chain is low-carbon. LNG has lower CO2 than oil, but methane slip raises its footprint. Green methanol and green ammonia need renewable electricity. Hydrogen from fossil gas is not automatically clean. Carbon intensity is emissions per unit of transport work.

sections.heading: Safety and bunkering
sections.text: Bunkering means supplying fuel to a ship. LNG needs cryogenic tanks, gas detection and training. Methanol is toxic and flammable. Ammonia is toxic and corrosive; hydrogen leaks easily and can embrittle metals. The IMO IGF Code gives international safety rules for low-flashpoint fuels; flag states and classification societies apply them. Ports need compatible terminals, trained crews and emergency plans.

sections.heading: Regulatory drivers
sections.text: MARPOL Annex VI limits sulphur and NOx and sets energy efficiency rules. IMO measures such as the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) and the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) push ships to cut carbon intensity; the IMO greenhouse gas strategy sets long-term aims. The EU includes shipping in its emissions trading system and has FuelEU Maritime. Exact limits and dates change, so check current IMO, flag state and port rules.

keyPoints: LNG is mainly methane, stored cryogenically; it cuts CO2, SOx and particulates but methane slip raises life-cycle emissions.
Methanol is a liquid fuel; green methanol needs renewable hydrogen and captured CO2.
Ammonia and hydrogen are carbon-free, but ammonia is toxic and hydrogen is flammable and hard to store.
Batteries suit short voyages and hybrids; fuel cells convert chemical energy directly to electricity.
Life-cycle emissions count the whole fuel chain, not only exhaust.
Energy = mass × LHV, so fuel mass = energy ÷ LHV; check IMO, flag state and port rules because limits change.

en.title: Research design and methods for a marine engineering dissertation
en.short: Designing, conducting and writing a master’s marine engineering dissertation.

sections.heading: Research design
sections.text: Research design is the plan linking a question to evidence. At master’s level, state the aim, objectives, research question or hypothesis, and the variables you will measure or interpret. Choose a design that fits the question: experiment, survey, case study, simulation or mixed methods. Explain sampling, validity (does the method measure what it claims?) and reliability (would it give the same result again?). Triangulation uses two or more methods or sources to strengthen a claim.

sections.heading: Literature review
sections.text: A literature review is not a list of summaries. Search journals, conference papers, classification society rules and company reports systematically, record your search terms, and group findings by theme. Critically compare methods and results, then identify the gap your dissertation addresses. Cite sources accurately and distinguish an author’s claim from established fact. Keep a reference manager from the start.

sections.heading: Methods and analysis
sections.text:
Quantitative methods produce numbers: measurements, experiments, surveys and simulation. Define instruments, calibration and uncertainty. Use descriptive statistics first, then inferential tests only when assumptions are met. Qualitative methods produce words: interviews, observations, documents and case studies. Record and code them into themes, and check interpretations with participants where possible. Mixed methods combine both. Analysis must answer the research question, not merely display data. State software and version, and keep raw data.

Case: Amaka studies fuel use on a Nigerian coastal ferry. Fuel and speed logs over 20 trips are paired with interviews of the chief engineer; triangulation tests whether the numbers and the account agree.

sections.heading: Ethics and writing
sections.text: Ethics covers informed consent, confidentiality, safety during sea trials, honest reporting and data storage. Obtain institutional approval before collecting data. Avoid plagiarism; acknowledge all sources. Write the dissertation as an argument: introduction, literature review, method, results, discussion, conclusion. Make the method reproducible enough for another engineer to repeat it. Check that every objective is answered. Follow your university’s formatting and submission rules, which vary by country and institution.

keyPoints: A research design links a clear question to evidence and states variables, sampling, validity and reliability.
A literature review synthesises sources by theme and identifies the gap, not just summarises papers.
Quantitative methods use measurement and statistics; qualitative methods use words and themes; mixed methods combine both.
Triangulation strengthens findings by comparing two or more methods or sources.
Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality, safety, honest reporting and institutional approval.
Write the dissertation as a structured argument and make the method reproducible.
